cocolog: myprog_step/4 -- prefix every predicate you define
why: There is no module system. `:- module/2' is accepted and IGNORED, and the eight vendored SWI libraries are consulted into the same store. Consult appends, so your clauses join theirs in one shared predicate record.
fix: prefix the head with the program's own name

swi: tcp_connect(_, _) :- ...   after :- use_module(library(tcp)); any loaded module's name
cocolog: a prefixed name
why: A loaded module's dispatcher answers a goal of its names before the knowledge base, so the program's clauses for one are dead code that listing/1 will happily show. A NAME OF THE ENGINE'S OR A COMPILED-IN MODULE'S IS NOT THIS SINCE 3.1.0: a program file's clauses take a non-ISO one over -- memberchk/2, format/2, msort/2 -- as swipl lets a user file define a system predicate, a library's call keeping the builtin; and the load refuses an ISO one's -- findall/3, write/1, is/2 -- with swipl's permission error, loudly.
empirical: cocolog -s F, F being :- use_module(library(tcp)). tcp_connect(a, b) :- write(mine), nl. main :- catch(tcp_connect(a, b), E, (print(caught(E)), nl)).  ==>  caught(error(domain_error(socket_address,a),context(tcp:tcp_connect/2,_G44))): the module answered, and mine was never written

cocolog: never define it
why: *->/2 is a control construct the step runs in place, before the builtin table and the store, so a program's clauses for it load, listing/1 shows them, and nothing calls them -- swipl compiles it inline and ignores them too, and so with the engine's own $ markers at any arity. Not the ISO constructs since 3.1.0 (once/1, call/N, catch/3, \+/1 ...): the load refuses their clauses, loudly, with swipl's permission error; nor not/1, ignore/1, trace/0 and notrace/0, which a program file takes over, as swipl calls them as the predicates they are there; nor a construct's name at an arity the step does not run it at (once/2), a predicate like any other.

cocolog: myprog_digit//1
why: A DCG head occupies arity+2, so `digit//1' is `digit/3' in the store -- which is dcg_basics' own. A blocklist built by a regex over heads is under-broad in exactly the arity that collides.

cocolog: "abc" IS [97,98,99] BY DEFAULT -- set the flag, or write 'abc'
why: double_quotes DEFAULTS to codes, so a bare "abc" is a code list. All four of SWI's values are settable now -- codes, chars, atom, string -- and the flag really changes what the reader builds, so `:- set_prolog_flag(double_quotes, string).' at the head of a file makes every "..." in it a string. The flag is per-MACHINE, not per-module: it is forced back to codes across a module load, so a program's choice cannot reach inside the vendored SWI files, which are written for codes.

cite.anchor: set_prolog_flag: double_quotes takes codes, chars, atom or string

fix: set the flag, or write 'abc', or str("abc") into a serialiser

cocolog: between/3, member/2, select/3, sub_atom/5, current_predicate/1 and nth0/3 DO backtrack, and since 3.28.0 retract/1 and clause/2 too
why: The first six are Prolog clauses in a library's Prolog half; retract/1 and clause/2 are constructs whose frame is retried as a call's, over the clauses that stood when they began. A C table entry answers once; clauses and those two answer again.

cite.anchor: '$between_n'(N, L, X) :- N1 is N - 1, M is L + 1, '$between_n'(N1, M, X).
sub_atom(A, B, L, Aft, Sub) :- '$sub_text_length'(A, B, L, Aft, Sub, N, atom), '$atom_byte_length'(A, NB), between(0, N, B)

swi: a defensive ! on every clause to force determinism
cocolog: omit it where the first arguments are distinct atoms, integers or functors; keep it where the caller may leave argument 1 unbound
why: First-argument indexing is live, and it is a semantics fact here rather than a speed one: a predicate whose first arguments are distinct atoms, integers or functors leaves no choice point. A cut added to force determinism the engine already gives you prunes solutions on the calls where argument 1 IS unbound. A float or a string first argument keys as 0, as an unbound one does, so there the walk and the choice point remain, unless another bound argument tells the clauses apart (swipl's JIT index, 3.24.0: of a predicate under eight clauses, the argument its assessment promises most of).

swi: :- initialization(main). with main :- ..., halt. -- the older script idiom -- run as cocolog -s FILE under a store
cocolog: :- initialization(main, main). or no directive at all, since -s calls main itself: under -s the file is a module whose load is muted, so a goal that a directive or initialization(G) runs during it writes nothing through, and a halt there ends the run before -s's own main has written anything
why: cocolog -s FILE is use_module(FILE), main, and a module's load is muted: its clauses, and what its load-time goals assert, belong to this process and not to the knowledge base. initialization(G, main) is the program rather than the load, so G runs unmuted; and a halt during a load commits whatever was written through, as a halt after the CLI's goal does. Under run FILE GOAL the file is consulted, not loaded as a module, and its load writes through, halt or none.
empirical: under --embed, on 1.8.57, a second process reading seen/1 back: -s of :- dynamic(seen/1). :- initialization(main). main :- assertz(seen(after_load)), halt. exits 0 and finds nothing; run FILE true finds seen(after_load); with :- initialization(main, main). instead, -s finds it too. :- assertz(seen(directive)). under -s is not kept even with no halt in the file, and is under run. Until 1.8.57 every halt during a load kept nothing, run or -s, --embed or a server.
fix: under -s, write from main -- the CLI's goal, or initialization(main, main) -- never from a directive or initialization(G)

cocolog: nothing: there is no tabling
why: table is a prefix operator at 1150 fx, as swipl's (since 3.2.0), so the directive parses and runs as a goal -- and table/1 is an unknown procedure: the load reports it and goes on with p/2 untabled, and a left-recursive definition that tabling would have ended loops for ever. thread_local, volatile, module_transparent and public are declarations since 3.2.0.
fix: delete the directive, and write p/2 so that it ends without tabling

cocolog: write nothing
why: Tier 1 is compiled in or preloaded at start-up: apply builtins dcg files library lists zigurat, plus assoc pairs ordsets yall aggregate ugraphs dcg_basics dcg_high_order. 26 such lines were deliberately removed from this tree.

cocolog: nothing -- it is tier 1 as dcg_basics
why: library(Dir/Name) becomes the path "Dir/Name", and the vendored file is lib/swipl/dcg_basics.pl. As a directive it is answered as loaded, by name: lb_carried lists dcg/basics, dcg/high_order and error, SWI's names for what this build carries under another arrangement. As a GOAL it raises.

cocolog: catch(G, error(T, _), ...)
why: A REFUSAL -- a library found and refused (a module that will not load), a module's own failure -- is the NON-ISO error(cocolog_error(Text), _), where the first argument is a sentence and not one of ISO's formals, so a handler that names a formal walks past it. A file or library that is NOT THERE is no refusal: it is swipl's error(existence_error(source_sink, Spec), _) since 3.4.0, where through 3.3.0 it was the sentence too. Neither loader ball matches error(T, context(_,_)) by its context: see row C3 for what the second argument actually holds.
fix: match error(T, _), and match cocolog_error/1 explicitly

swi: assuming error/2's context is always context(Name/Arity, _)
cocolog: a core builtin's is swipl's, context(system:Name/Arity, Message), since 3.0.0, and a loadable module's own predicate's names the module, context(Module:Name/Arity, _), since 3.0.2, as swipl names a foreign predicate's; the loader's ball leaves it UNBOUND, and the house style of a library puts a bare Name/Arity there
why: MEASURED, not read: catch(atom_length(_,_), error(T,C), true) binds C to context(system:atom_length/2,_), swipl 9.0.4's term, and an uncaught one prints swipl's `atom_length/2: ' before its message; after use_module(library(sha)), catch(sha_hash(foo,abc,_), error(T,C), true) binds C to context(sha:sha_hash/3,_), and the message begins `sha:sha_hash/3: '. The loader's ball -- error(existence_error(source_sink, Spec), _) for a file that is not there, as swipl's, or error(cocolog_error(Text), _) for one found and refused -- leaves the slot unbound, so context(_,_) matches it by BINDING and reads nothing; a library that throws the house form error(type_error(a,b), my/2) is not matched by context(_,_) at all. Through 2.16 every builtin left it unbound, and through 3.0.1 every loadable module's. Card row C2 is about the first argument.
empirical: cocolog --local query "catch(atom_length(_,_), error(T,C), true), write(T-C), nl"  ==>  instantiation_error-context(system:atom_length/2,_G50)
fix: match error(T, _); read the context of a core builtin's or a loadable module's error only, and never depend on its shape elsewhere

cocolog: every option of swipl's table is applied as swipl's -- max_depth(D) since 3.49.0, fullstop(true), nl(true), dotlists(true) and no_lists(true) since 3.53.0, portray(true) and portray_goal(G) since 3.54.0, and character_escapes(B), character_escapes_unicode(B), quote_non_ascii(B), brace_terms(B) and cycles(B) since 3.55.0 -- but attributes(_) and blobs(_), which are checked and read past
why: write_term/2 applies quoted(true), ignore_ops(true), variable_names(Names) (since 1.10.6), numbervars(true) (since 2.2.5), spacing(next_argument), priority(P), max_depth(D) (since 3.49.0), fullstop(B), nl(B), dotlists(B) and no_lists(B) (since 3.53.0), portray(B) and portray_goal(G) (since 3.54.0, the hook asked of each term but a variable as swipl's pl-write.c asks it), and character_escapes(B) (false: the quoted text as it is, its quote doubled), character_escapes_unicode(B) (false: `\x1\'), quote_non_ascii(B) (true: a name past U+00FF quoted), brace_terms(B) (false: `{}(T)') and cycles(B) (false: domain_error(cyclic_term, T)) (since 3.55.0) as swipl's, and checks every option of swipl's table for its type, as swipl's does; cocolog has no attributed variable and no blob, so attributes(_) and blobs(_) say nothing to a write of its and are read past.

cocolog: functor(T,'.',2) or T = [_|_]
why: A list cell is './2' here, not SWI 7's '[|]'/2.

swi: --> Codes with a bound code list in the body
cocolog: walk it: raw([]) --> []. / raw([C|Cs]) --> [C], raw(Cs).
why: A body item that is a VARIABLE is a call: it translates to phrase(Cs,S0,S), which calls a predicate named after the list's head rather than emitting the list.

cocolog: the predicates all exist now; "abc" is still a CODE LIST
why: The string type is real: string/1, string_concat/3, split_string/4, sub_string/5, atom_string/2, string_to_atom/2, number_string/2, string_codes/2, string_chars/2, term_string/2, text_concat/3, string_length/2 and string_lower/upper all answer, and a code list is accepted anywhere text is wanted. What the READER does is a flag: double_quotes DEFAULTS to codes, so "abc" is [97,98,99] and string("abc") is FALSE in a file that said nothing, where SWI says true. `:- set_prolog_flag(double_quotes, string).' at the head of a file changes that for the rest of it -- the flag takes all four of SWI's values -- so a string is either MADE or asked for, never written by default.

cite.anchor: set_prolog_flag: double_quotes takes codes, chars, atom or string

fix: atom_string(abc, S) to make one; "abc" is still codes

swi: open/3,4  close/1  read/1  read_term/2,3  nl/1  write/2  current_output/1
cocolog: no stream layer in the engine; library(stream) supplies them, and a file that loads it -- or library(websocket), which loads it -- is not flagged
why: The engine has no streams: format/3 takes a SINK, and the read path is read_file_to_codes/2 and a DCG -- unless the file loads library(stream), which gives open/3,4, close/1, get_char/2, read_term/2,3, write/2, nl/1, current_output/1, set_output/1 and the rest their ISO meanings over a table of its own, and lifts this trap; library(websocket) loads it and lifts it too, its sessions ending with the message close(Code, Why). (see/1, seen/0, tell/1 and told/0 are absent either way, and are left out of this pattern because they are ordinary words: `seen(X)' is somebody's own predicate far more often than it is Edinburgh I/O.)
fix: :- use_module(library(stream)). -- or read_file_to_codes/2 plus a DCG, and format/3 with a sink

swi: predsort/3 assertion/1 freeze/2 dif/2 when/2 call_with_inference_limit/3
cocolog: absent; the last is deliberately spelled call_limited/3
why: Deliberately absent so ported code errors instead of silently differing: SWI's call_with_inference_limit leaves the goal's choice points alive and call_limited/3 commits to the first solution, and a predicate that agrees with SWI until it does not is worse than one that never claimed to.

cocolog: fails -- twenty flags answer: executable, argv, os_argv, double_quotes, text_units, bounded, max_integer, min_integer, max_tagged_integer, min_tagged_integer, float_overflow, float_zero_div, float_undefined, float_underflow, float_min, float_max, float_max_integer, verbose, optimise_unify, stack_limit
why: There is no flag table. TWENTY flags answer -- executable, argv, os_argv, double_quotes, text_units, since 2.0.0 bounded (true), max_integer, min_integer, max_tagged_integer and min_tagged_integer, since 2.2.2 swipl's four float flags and its three float bounds, since 2.16.0 verbose (normal), since 3.15.0 optimise_unify (true), and since 3.32.0 stack_limit (1073741824) -- and every other one FAILS, so a portability shim written against current_prolog_flag/2 takes the wrong branch, silently. double_quotes, text_units (characters or bytes), the four float flags, verbose (any atom; silent quiets print_message/2's informational and banner kinds), optimise_unify (swipl's booleans) and stack_limit (bytes; a negative one none) are the ones a program can also SET, by set_prolog_flag/2 as a goal since 2.2.2, which refuses every other flag: existence_error(prolog_flag, F) where swipl by default makes the flag, and permission_error(modify, flag, F) for the read-only ones, argv and os_argv among them. Three are questions about the process, the five integer flags about the integers, 64 bits wide, and the float bounds are swipl's.
fix: do not branch on a flag

swi: assuming a :- use_module(library(tcp)). header loaded something
cocolog: probe by CALLING inside catch/3
why: Since 1.8.39 a directive whose library is not on the path is REPORTED at load, in SWI's two lines -- `source_sink `library(tcp)' does not exist', then `Goal (directive) failed' (before, it answered success in total silence) -- but the load GOES ON, as SWI's does, and the program runs without the library. The absence surfaces again at the first call as existence_error(procedure, tcp_listen/2), naming the predicate and not the module, so a program that must run where the module was not built still probes.
empirical: a file whose only directive is use_module(library(no_such_library_at_all)) prints `ERROR: F:1:' and `source_sink `library(no_such_library_at_all)' does not exist', then the Warning `Goal (directive) failed: user:use_module(library(no_such_library_at_all))', swipl 9.0.4's four lines to the letter, and runs to completion with exit 0; the same term as a goal raises error(existence_error(source_sink, library(no_such_library_at_all)), _), swipl's ball (through 3.3.0 error(cocolog_error('use_module: library(no_such_library_at_all): not found on the library path'), _))
fix: probe as a goal inside catch/3

swi: current_predicate/1 as an availability probe for a library
cocolog: catch existence_error around the real call
why: current_predicate/1 is about the KNOWLEDGE BASE, and a module's predicates are not clauses in it -- so it says no for a library that is loaded and working. Named whole it answers for the system's own since 3.31.0 -- a construct, a row of the engine or of a compiled-in module -- and still never for a library's or a loadable module's. The same flag is what makes the collision oracle work.

swi: one long clause, or one big atom asserted
cocolog: chunk at <= 3800 bytes and assert the completion mark in the same turn
why: A row must fit inside a page: measured, a clause of 8013 characters stores and 8014 comes back `allocation overflow'. It USED to be worse than the documented refusal -- the throw arrived at COMMIT and took every other clause of the transaction with it, and under --embed the writing process reported nothing at all: exit 0, empty stderr, and the clause simply not there when the next process looked. Since 1.1.0 the store refuses it on the way in, one clause at a time and named, so `assertz/1' raises resource_error(clause_length) and a consult reports it and carries on; since 1.2.0 the budget is derived rather than fixed -- `page - 190 - len(kb) - len(name)', measured at three page sizes and three name lengths -- and the embedded engine is asked its page while a server's is assumed to be the default unless $COCOLOG_PAGE_SIZE says otherwise -- 8192 until 1.10.0, and 65536 since, when a store began keeping its page beside it (DIR/pagesize; a store made before keeps 8192). This rule's own 7800 sits below all of that on purpose: a linter has no store to ask. THE ADVICE IS UNCHANGED: a clause this long still cannot be stored, and an error you have to catch is not a place to put a design. A single term over 65535 bytes fails earlier and differently, in the client.

cite.anchor: a Text of 8192 comes back as `allocation overflow'
a Text is limited to 65535 bytes
WHAT A ROW WILL HOLD, MEASURED AND NOT GUESSED

empirical: cocolog --embed ./KB run t.pl main, with t.pl holding big('x' x N), on an 8192-byte store (every store before 1.10.0). Bisected 3000/4000/5000/6000/7000/7500/7900/8000/8010/8011/8020/8100: the clause TEXT stores at 8013 characters and is refused at 8014. Before 1.1.0 both writes exited 0 with empty stderr and N>=8020 read back as existence_error(procedure, big/1); now the write raises error(resource_error(clause_length), _) and the clauses asserted beside it are still there for the next process.

cocolog: cocolog run prog.pl helpers.pl main
why: With more than one argument after `run', the LAST is the goal. Otherwise helpers.pl is read as a term to prove.
